---
title: "Three time axes"
---

Every measure carries two notions of "when" in its columns, and the release
you attached is a third. Conflating them is the characteristic error in this
domain.

| Axis | Column(s) | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Period** | `period_start`, `period_end` | the time the estimate *describes* |
| **Source release** | `source_release` | the upstream edition that *published* it |
| **Cancer Basemap release** | the folder you attach (`v2026-11-02/`, or `latest/`) | which monthly bundle you are reading |

## A real example: PLACES 2024 vs. 2025

Press **Run** to execute a block in your browser against the latest release.

```{.sql .runnable}
SELECT source_release, period_start, period_end, value
FROM measure.observation
WHERE source = 'PLACES' AND measure_id = 'PLACES:CANCER:age_adjusted'
  AND geo_id = 'county:08031'
ORDER BY source_release
```

Two rows, same measure, same county (Denver County, CO). The **source
release** is `'2024'` or `'2025'`, the PLACES edition. The **period** each
release describes is one year *earlier*: the 2024 release models
2022 BRFSS data, the 2025 release models 2023 data. A query that filters on
`source_release = '2025'` expecting "2025 data" is filtering on the release
label, not the period. The value it gets describes 2023.

Both source releases are in every Cancer Basemap release, because
`source_release` is a column, not a folder. The **Cancer Basemap release** is
the third axis: a bundle holds the current rows only, so if a source corrects
a value within one `source_release`, the corrected row replaces the old one in
the next bundle. The earlier value stays in the earlier release, which is why a
dated folder, or its Hugging Face tag, is how you reproduce an analysis (see
[Versions and citation](/guides/versions-and-citation.qmd)).

## A second example: an edition's own period moves

SVI's `source_release` **is** the edition, and each edition's own period is
a five-year ACS window that moves with it, never the edition year alone. This
reads Colorado's counties only (`geo_id LIKE 'county:08%'`), which is enough to
show every edition's period:

```{.sql .runnable}
SELECT source_release AS edition, min(period_start) AS period_start, max(period_end) AS period_end
FROM measure.observation
WHERE source = 'SVI' AND geo_id LIKE 'county:08%'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1
```

The 2020 edition's period is `2016`–`2020`, not `'2020'` alone. Treating an
edition's release year as its period would be off by up to four years.

## Why this matters for a catchment report

The sentence a cancer center has to defend, *"in our catchment, as reported
by source S in release R, the measure was X"*, names the release, not the
period, on purpose: the release is what you can point back to when someone
asks "where did this number come from." Reproducing a past analysis means
filtering on `source_release`, not on `period_start`/`period_end` (a later
release can restate an earlier period with revised numbers), and pinning the
Cancer Basemap release you attached, since a bundle's rows can change between
releases.
